content:
Global public debt is about to reach 100% of world gross domestic product, the highest level since the aftermath of World War II, the head of the International Monetary Fund warned on Thursday, calling for "urgent attention" to government finances.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva delivered the warning at the plenary session of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit in Shenzhen, China, where the world's largest economies were meeting against a backdrop of rising borrowing costs and a fresh bout of inflation.

"The level of global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II. This requires urgent attention," Georgieva said, according to [MercoPress](https://en.mercopress.com/2026/11/19/imf-warns-global-debt-will-soon-reach-100-of-gdp-the-highest-since-world-war-ii).

The warning is deliberately stark, but the IMF's own published numbers give it an important qualification. The Fund's Fiscal Affairs Department said in Bangkok on October 14 that global public debt stood at about 94% of GDP in 2025 and is expected to approach 100% only by 2029. Georgieva's "soon" is therefore a political message as much as a forecast: the direction of travel is set, the milestone is within sight, and governments should act before they arrive at it rather than after.

What has changed since the IMF last set out its debt outlook is the cost of carrying that debt. Georgieva told the APEC leaders that a rebound in global inflation, driven both by the energy crisis caused by the war in the Middle East and by surging demand linked to the construction of artificial intelligence infrastructure, has pushed many countries to raise interest rates. Bond yields in many advanced economies are now at their highest in decades, according to reporting from Shenzhen, and every extra point on a yield curve is an extra bill for a finance ministry already running a deficit.

That is the trap Georgieva was describing. Debt accumulated during the pandemic, when governments borrowed heavily to keep economies afloat, is now being refinanced at far higher rates, while wars and trade tensions keep pushing energy prices up. The result is that interest payments are eating a growing share of public budgets, leaving less room for investment, welfare or the infrastructure spending that might help economies grow their way out of the problem.

Artificial intelligence sits on both sides of the ledger. Georgieva told the summit that 2026 has been the first year in which AI has had a tangible impact on global growth, and she put global growth at 3.1% this year, with the APEC region growing faster at 3.4% and world trade expanding by 4.6%. But she also warned that the AI boom itself is being financed in a way that should worry policymakers: more than $1 trillion of so-called circular financing between AI companies, of which roughly two-thirds is supported by debt, according to reporting of her remarks.

The concern is straightforward. When AI firms lend to each other, buy each other's products and book each other's spending as revenue, the growth looks real in the national accounts but rests on a chain of borrowing. If one link in that chain breaks, the losses cascade. It is a risk the IMF chief raised alongside the public debt warning, and it connects directly to the market anxiety visible this week, when technology shares led a [global stock sell-off](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/global-stocks-worst-run-since-2023-ai-selloff-november-2026) that has now run for five straight sessions.

Georgieva's prescription is one she has repeated for months: growth alone will not solve the problem. In her words to policymakers, economic growth "by itself" cannot pull countries out of the debt hole, and fiscal discipline is also required. The sooner governments take the hard decisions on spending and revenue, she has argued, the better, because delay means the debt is refinanced at higher rates and the adjustment, when it eventually comes, is sharper.

What that means in practice differs sharply by country. Advanced economies with deep bond markets can still borrow, but at yields that punish complacency; emerging economies face a harder choice between cutting public investment and paying more to roll over their debts. The IMF's message to both groups is the same: use the current period of still-solid growth, which the Fund puts at 3.1% for 2026, to start consolidating public finances, rather than waiting for the next downturn to force the issue.

The warning also lands at a moment when governments are being asked to spend more, not less. Defence budgets are rising across Europe and Asia, climate adaptation demands vast investment, and the AI race itself is driving states to subsidise chip plants and data centres. Each of those claims on the public purse is defensible on its own; together, they are the reason debt ratios keep climbing even in years when economies are growing.

Markets will be watching what happens next. The IMF's next fiscal outlook will show whether the 2029 date for the 100% milestone has moved closer, and finance ministers in the APEC bloc will face questions about how they intend to respond to Georgieva's call. For now, the significance of her Shenzhen speech is that the world's most senior economic official has chosen to frame the debt problem not as a distant risk but as an imminent one, and to link it explicitly to the two forces shaping the global economy: the return of inflation and the rise of artificial intelligence.

If she is right, the coming years will test whether governments can do two difficult things at once: keep borrowing to fund the energy transition, defence and the AI build-out, while bringing debt ratios down from levels not seen since the world was rebuilding after a war. The [take-private wave](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/tpg-corpay-bill-6-billion-buyout-november-2026) sweeping corporate America shows that private capital is already repricing risk; Georgieva's message is that public finances cannot escape the same repricing for much longer. As [TechTimes reported](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/331182/20261120/kristalina-georgieva-urges-tighter-policy-ai-lifts-inflation-imf-forecast-credits-energy-most.htm), the IMF expects global inflation to reach 4.7% this year, a level that keeps the pressure on central banks to hold rates higher for longer, and on governments to pay more for every dollar they borrow.
summary: IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva told APEC leaders in Shenzhen that global public debt is about to reach 100% of world GDP, the highest level since World War II, warning that higher interest rates are making the burden harder to carry.
title: IMF warns global public debt will soon hit 100% of world GDP, highest since World War II
